column2: “Shot himself?”

“His grades were too good, his thinking too acute. While studying dragon lore, he got trapped in certain philosophical difficulties and couldn’t find his way out. So he shot himself. That was when we added psychological counselors,” Masashi Toyama said.
“Sounds promising.” Lu Mingfei drew a breath. “I’ve always been famous for being slow.”
“But you have potential!” Professor Guderian gave Toyama an exuberant thumbs-up, clearly indicating that his student was the best.
Lu Mingfei couldn’t understand what there was to celebrate. He wanted to cover his face.

“We’ve brought two pieces of evidence proving that dragons exist. Both are high-grade artifacts we borrowed especially from the college archives.” With a passcode and fingerprint, Toyama opened the first case. Beneath layers of foam lay a black scale, about half the size of a palm, perfectly shield-shaped, its surface gleaming as though freshly oiled. Fine patterns showed clearly beneath the sheen.
“Feel it,” Toyama said.

Lu Mingfei cautiously picked it up. It felt artificial, rather like steel—cold and tough, yet almost as light as plastic. Its edge was sharp enough to cut his fingers at the slightest pressure. Then Toyama pressed something into his hand.
He stared. It was a handgun.

“Walther PPK. Seven-point-six-five-millimeter caliber, muzzle velocity two hundred eighty meters per second, effective range fifty meters. The Equipment Department made a few improvements. Now you can shoot the scale.” Toyama set it on the windowsill.
“I know this gun… James Bond uses it.” Lu Mingfei’s face was white.
“Yes, the classic Bond pistol.” Toyama covered his ears. “Don’t worry. Just fire. Aim at the scale.”
“Lunatic logic is impossible to understand.” Miserably, Lu Mingfei raised the gun. Following his high school military training, he aimed at the scale, gritted his teeth, and pulled the trigger.

A thunderous blast. It felt as though a sledgehammer had hit his chest. The PPK’s recoil was like firing an aircraft cannon. He toppled backward into the sofa, stars filling his vision, nearly losing consciousness.
“So he isn’t one of the physically gifted students!” Toyama’s surprised voice sounded beside him. “Perhaps I should have brought an ordinary revolver.”
“Was that gun modified by Equipment? Honestly, don’t casually test things those lunatics have worked on!” Professor Guderian complained repeatedly.
“I was curious. It’s a fine gun. It might not blow a dragon’s eye apart with one shot, but it should leave a mark on fourth- or fifth-generation dragons,” Toyama said.

Lu Mingfei shook his head hard until his surroundings came into focus. First, Professor Guderian’s concerned face. Second, the black scale swaying in Toyama’s hand. Perfect and unblemished. Nothing had marked its surface. He was absolutely certain he had hit its center. He wasn’t an athletic student, but in military training he had been one of the rare shooters to score a hundred with ten shots. His instructor had been astonished that this unremarkable boy handled a gun so well.
A pistol comparable to an aircraft cannon hadn’t pierced that scale.

“A dragon scale. Sven Hedin found it in 1900, in the ruins of Loulan in Xinjiang. He didn’t recognize it, but discovered that neither fire nor hammer blows could damage it, so he took it from China to Europe. Someone there recognized it: Meinhard Cassell. That’s our first piece of evidence. Beginning to believe us?” Toyama asked.
“Couldn’t it be high technology?” Lu Mingfei still resisted.
“Even a titanium alloy made using nanotechnology couldn’t stop that shot,” Toyama said. “I have a doctorate in materials science from the University of Tokyo. Trust me.”
Not just lunatics everywhere. Highly educated lunatics everywhere, Lu Mingfei thought.
“Now, the second piece of evidence.” Toyama opened the other case. A cylindrical glass jar appeared before Lu Mingfei, like the specimen jars his biology teacher used.

His mouth fell open as though he had been struck by lightning. If Toyama had stuffed an orange into it, he probably wouldn’t have noticed. Suspended in pale-yellow formalin was a lizardlike animal, yellowish-white, its long tail curled around it like a fetus in the womb. Long whiskers drifted slowly beside its mouth. With its eyes closed, it looked peaceful as a baby. Without the two membranous wings spread from its back, he would have taken it for some ancient lizard.

“A red dragon hatchling. It isn’t even dead, merely dormant. Dragons are difficult to kill, especially the noble first and second generations. Even destroying their bodies cannot destroy their souls. They can awaken again,” Toyama said. “An exceedingly rare specimen. Humans usually can’t capture dragons. They sense the activity of our brains and attack or flee before we approach. This specimen was discovered in India in 1796. Fortunately, a giant python seems to have swallowed it just after it hatched. Local farmers killed the python and found the hatchling in its stomach.”
“Are you sure it isn’t plastic?” Lu Mingfei covered his face. “It’s over. My entire worldview’s finished.”
“Look closely. The detail, the patterns on its scales. What artist could make a plastic model this perfect?” Toyama brought the jar nearer.

Now only half a centimeter of glass separated their faces. Its wings and whiskers stirred in the liquid, as though it hovered among clouds. Toyama was right. Those details, those patterns, were too real. Only nature or God could create something like this. Such creatures existed in history’s shadows, in different peoples’ legends, at the limits of human imagination—and inside this sealed glass jar.
“Perfect, isn’t it?” Toyama sounded admiring.
“Perfect,” Lu Mingfei murmured.
He stared at the membranes covering its eyes and remembered those golden pupils opening slowly in the dark, as though the gates of the world were opening before him.

The hatchling in the formalin suddenly opened its golden eyes. Its whole body jerked from head to tail. Stretching its neck, it roared at Lu Mingfei. Burning dragonfire ignited deep in its throat and burst out! It spread its wings fiercely, trying to break free of the jar. Awake now, though no larger than a cat, it possessed a dragon’s majesty.
Lu Mingfei didn’t dodge. All three stood stupefied, watching the ancient specimen revive.

The tiny flame died at once. Formalin flooded the hatchling’s throat, making it cough in agony like a drowning man. Nor could it break the glass. Its powerful wingbeats left not even a mark. This awakening, centuries in the making, ended as quickly as it had begun. Soon the hatchling curled up again, peaceful once more, returning to dormancy.
“Aaaaaaah!” At last, Lu Mingfei could scream. Trembling, he pointed at the jar.
“Don’t shout,” Professor Guderian murmured.
“Didn’t you see? Didn’t you see? It came alive! It came alive! A living dragon!” Lu Mingfei shook the utterly stunned old man and yelled.
“I saw.” The professor turned to Toyama. “You saw it, too, didn’t you?”

White-faced, Toyama could only nod. “Yes… But that really wasn’t what I meant to do. I didn’t know it would wake up just now…” His voice suddenly rose almost to a shriek. “What happened? Did those people in the archives mislabel it? Its awakening date is supposed to be 2077! Their careless labels could kill us! It breathed dragonfire just now! Dragonfire!”

“Thank goodness we began switching to nanomaterial containers two years ago. Otherwise it wouldn’t have held…” Cold sweat covered the professor’s forehead. “Heavens. Professor Manstein and I calculated its awakening date. We shouldn’t have been wrong… Unless… unless it was a bloodline summons!”
“A bloodline summons?” Toyama turned to Lu Mingfei, plainly regarding a monster.
“What else could wake a dragon early?” The professor’s eyes blazed as he thumped Lu Mingfei’s shoulder. “Your powerful bloodline called to it! Now do you understand how extraordinary you are?”
His shoulder was nearly collapsing under the blows. “What are you talking about? Don’t blame me for a potentially fatal accident! I didn’t do anything!”
“The Dragon Emperor can make humans submit merely by looking at them. You needn’t do anything. You’re a dragon hybrid with second-generation capabilities!” The professor nodded vigorously.
“What hybrid? My dad’s human. My mom’s human. Read too many Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio? Think everyone in China has babies with dragons?” Lu Mingfei argued.

“No. They are indeed human. But both are dragon hybrids, so your blood contains a substantial proportion of dragon blood.” Guderian exchanged a glance with Toyama. “You’ll learn sooner or later. Most people at this college are hybrids. Do you know how we determine rank? By bloodline! You’re S-rank because your dragon blood is exceptionally pure!”
Lu Mingfei was dumbstruck. Suddenly the professor looked like an old dragon, liable to breathe deadly fire into his face at any moment.

What was this place? A whole college of dragon hybrids? How was that different from a dragon’s nest? And in that nest, he was… a little white rabbit! His dragon blood was pure? Why had a fine young mammal raised under the red flag suddenly been classified as a reptile?

“Your proportion of dragon blood does not exceed fifty percent, though. We don’t admit students above that. Their potential far exceeds ordinary people’s, but the dragon blood slowly turns them into followers of dragons,” the professor said.
“You have… a grudge against dragons?”

“Humanity does. Not just us.” His eyes shone. “Your Dragon Genealogy course will explain everything. Now that you know dragons exist, would you like to learn more? There’s a way! Every course includes knowledge about them. Why don’t we choose your classes?”
“I don’t want to learn more! Can I withdraw?” Lu Mingfei raised a hand.

The professor looked disappointed. “Well… You can. But the agreement you signed includes memory erasure. If you withdraw, these memories must be removed. Having glimpsed the real world, wouldn’t it be a shame to leave?”
“What shame?” Lu Mingfei asked.
“Who wouldn’t want to know the real world? It’s broader than you can imagine. Beside it, the world you knew is as tiny as a grain of rice on a wasteland,” Toyama said.
Lu Mingfei paused, then immediately shook his head. “No. Don’t want to. I’ve never minded being a fat, white rice weevil.”

“It isn’t just memory loss.” The professor patted his shoulder. “Think. Your parents are of dragon blood. Your uncle and aunt don’t like you. You have no particular talents. If your memory’s erased and you’re sent back to China, you’ll have to repeat a year for the entrance exam. Can you imagine how miserable that would be?”
The old man had struck his weakness exactly. Compared with some grand, authentic world, the pressure of repeating the college entrance exam was real to him—terrifyingly real.
His face fell. “All right. I’ll try it for a couple of days…”

“Excellent!” Excitement flashed in the professor’s eyes. “I already have your training plan! For the first semester, I recommend Introduction to Dragon Genealogy, Magic-Powered Mechanical Design I, and Alchemical Chemistry I as your major courses. Take Old Norse for your language elective, and Tai Chi for PE. That gives you thirteen credits. No other freshman should match you. I’ll make you Cassell’s second truly deserving S-rank student in more than forty years!”

“Higher expectations? Parents like these don’t understand their son at all. Do they think they gave birth to a genius?” Lu Mingfei felt utterly powerless. “All right. Let’s stop talking around it. What if I fail?”

“Just retake the course. Unless you seriously violate the rules, Cassell doesn’t expel students. Some fail for years and still keep retaking the exams.” The professor sounded reassuring. “Remember Fingel? He’s been in his fourth year for four years… Nobody told him to leave.”

Reassurance? This was a naked threat. Fingel had once been a spirited A-rank student. Now he had been tormented into a sleazy vagrant. And that S-rank senior had shot himself. Apparently, the higher your rank, the more likely you were to die, Lu Mingfei thought.
“Fine. I agree. I’ll sign. One last question: why is Chinese compulsory? Why do you all speak it?”

“An excellent question.” The professor nodded. “According to the Research Department, several heavyweight figures among the dragons, at the rank of prince, lie dormant in China. They’re about to awaken. Chinese became compulsory ten years ago. Every one of you bears the duty of entering China’s heartland to kill Dragon Kings!”
“No wonder you assign jobs after graduation… You couldn’t recruit anyone for work like this!” Lu Mingfei said.
“But our benefits are excellent. We even pay for your medical insurance!”
“Please! You’re in the dragon-slaying business. How could anyone live without medical insurance? This work could kill you! What’s the maximum coverage? Fifty million dollars?”
“It covers flying your remains back to China, free of charge…”
“What?” His eyes widened. He imagined a corpse under a white sheet being carried off a plane, a tag on its head bearing the familiar name Lu Mingfei.

Flanked by Professor Guderian and Masashi Toyama, both clapping his shoulders heartily, he left the office like a wilted chicken. Men dressed as maintenance workers passed them with toolboxes, apparently heading to repair the window in which the aircraft-cannon PPK had blasted a large hole.

Outside the medieval-style building were green lawns, crimson cobbled paths, and castle-like buildings. Pigeons rose and settled on a distant church roof. Sunlight restored a little of Lu Mingfei’s vitality. At least it looked as though he still lived in the human world.
“My mom…” he began.

He needed to find out exactly what role his parents had played in this enrollment fiasco. What parents could be scheming enough to torment their only son to death? Had they found him abandoned? It hadn’t felt that way when he was little.
A piercing alarm suddenly tore through the air, echoing across campus like a ghost racing and howling. Lu Mingfei froze. The two men’s instantly grave expressions clearly signaled trouble.
“Huh? An air raid?” He looked around. “Dragons attacking? Do dragons carry out air raids? Right, they can fly!”

Only after saying it did he realize he had accepted Cassell’s premise that dragons existed. He also noticed something strange. The enormous campus was empty. Only the three of them stood beside the lawn. Even if summer vacation wasn’t over, that was unreasonable.
“Damn… Forgot what day it is… Find cover! Shit, they’re about to start!” Toyama shouted.
“Back to the office!” the professor said grimly.

Too late. People in black combat uniforms, carrying M4-series rifles, appeared on the building’s stairs behind them. Maintenance workers rushed out of the office, apparently to stop them. The others raised their weapons and fired. The burly carpenters, built like special-forces soldiers, fell the instant they emerged.
Looks like his insurance for shipping his remains home would come in handy right away.

Before the guns turned toward them, Toyama dragged Lu Mingfei and the professor into a narrow passage. The black-clad intruders ignored them completely and raced past. People in dark-red combat uniforms poured from the church. This utterly silent campus abruptly became a battlefield. Armed figures streamed from every building, grouping by uniform color and spraying one another mercilessly. Many dropped the instant they appeared. The gunfire was deafening. Lu Mingfei almost thought he was on a North African battlefield in World War II.
He couldn’t speak. He could only stare at the professor.
“What does the Student Council president think he’s doing? What’s his name again? Does he want to lose credits?” Guderian covered his ears and roared at Toyama.

“Has he ever cared? His GPA’s already low!” Toyama ducked nimbly. A bullet whistled over his head. A real bullet, Lu Mingfei was sure. A fraction slower, and Toyama would have fallen like the maintenance men. A Student Council uprising? Did these students consider armed conflict their vocation?
“Caesar Gattuso!” Toyama straightened angrily. “That spoiled brat with the Bugatti Veyron!”
He drew his aircraft-cannon PPK and changed the magazine, his face set with a commando’s resolve before battle.
“I’ll remember him! If he takes my class, I’ll make him regret it!” Guderian shouted.

As he spoke, his life ended. A bullet struck his body with tremendous force, leaving a smoking hole in his shabby suit. Blood splashed out. He lowered his head and painfully examined the wound, then seized Lu Mingfei and said only, “Your course selection form… Remember to fill it in!”
He collapsed. Toyama tried to rush to help, but a bullet struck his back. As though someone had shoved him, he lurched forward several steps and never rose again.
Surely… this can’t be a joke? Lu Mingfei thought. People had died, unmistakably, right before him.

Back pressed to the wall, he felt countless trajectories crossing outside, murderous bullets whipping past. The campus was a slaughterhouse. He was only a freshman, not even assigned a room yet. He didn’t know which side were dragons and which humans. Trembling, he felt his head was full of paste. If a bullet pierced it now, whatever sprayed out certainly wouldn’t be brains.
“Locate them! Locate them! Forty-three enemies left!”
“Twenty-seven left! One sniper unlocated! Thirteen of ours down! Take that sniper out!”

Both sides roared into radios while firing continuously. Strangely, nobody tried to enter his passage. Only stray shots kept coming. He stood rigid beside Guderian’s and Toyama’s bodies, imagining himself a peaceable wooden post.

Who knew how long the slaughter lasted? Smoke covered the campus. Bodies littered lawns and paths. Both sides had deployed grenades, grenade dischargers, shoulder-fired rockets, and more. He had browsed enough weapons magazines to recognize the expensive hardware. Bullets shattered a row of nearby windows, once again demolishing his hope that this was merely an exercise.
Those weapons were the real thing!

His pulse approached a limit of a hundred eighty beats a minute. Adrenaline flowed like sweat… He could die any second, yet somehow nothing happened… nothing… nothing… Exhausted, he crouched with his chin in his hands and watched. Gradually he grasped the situation. The black and dark-red teams were enemies, each trying to storm the other’s headquarters. Black’s was the small building they had just left; Red’s was the church across the lawn. Fire centered on the parking lot between them. Assault teams had to cross it, but there was insufficient cover. Fully exposed to the barrage, more than forty people had died there.

“If you were Zerg, charging like that would make sense. You spawn fast and have no brains. But as Terran, shouldn’t you siege some tanks and shell the position first? Or send a Ghost to drop a nuke?” he thought wildly.

As though a commander had understood StarCraft master Lu Mingfei’s intentions, a Red fighter appeared, trying to cross the lot with a black briefcase. After nimbly dodging several barrages, he was knocked down by a sniper’s shot from above. The overturned case bore a clear yellow nuclear symbol.
Lu Mingfei’s face twitched. “I was only saying… You actually have one? Not bad, I guess… A nuclear blast this close probably wouldn’t hurt.”
Hopeless. A battlefield for lunatics was beyond a normal person like him.
Gunfire thinned. Smoke cleared a little. A powerful, resonant voice sounded from every direction through the public-address system. “Caesar, how many have you got left? Still going?”
“Not bad, Chu Zihang.” The reply came over the same system, with a cold hint of laughter. “Just me and one girl left. Want me to send the girl charging in?”
“Chu Zihang?” Lu Mingfei paused. The name sounded very familiar.

“I’ve only got one girl left, too. Unfortunately for you, she’s that sniper giving you trouble. As long as she covers the lot, you can’t cross. Unfortunately for me, she isn’t much good at charging either.”
“Surely we won’t have a stalemate this year? What a pity.”
“It would be. I wanted to win your Bugatti.”
“All I have left now is a hunting knife. You?”
“Murasame, of course. My command sword.”
“See you in the parking lot.”
“Good.”

The loudspeakers’ electrical hiss abruptly stopped. Both cut communications. The campus was quiet as a dead city, gun smoke hanging like morning mist. In his passage, Lu Mingfei looked around, sensing something bad approaching. After considering, he lay beside Toyama and Guderian. Turning toward the old man’s face, he remembered that he had been kind to him, only to be killed for no reason. A little sadness stirred.
“Your own fault, working at such a weird college.” He sighed and laid Guderian’s arm across his back, making it look as though they had been shot together while the professor tried to shield him.
The church doors and those of the small building opened at once. Heavy combat boots took their first steps almost simultaneously.

The red-clad man carried a military hunting knife about half a meter long, gold patterns branded onto its black blade. The black-clad man held a long Japanese sword reflecting dazzling sunlight. They approached the parking lot, their measured footsteps drawing the tension tighter and tighter.
“What now? Hand-to-hand? You charge in carrying miniature nukes, then fight hand-to-hand?” Lu Mingfei thought.

At one edge of the lot, the red-clad man removed his mask. Brilliant golden hair fell around a face like a Greek sculpture. His rare ice-blue eyes were cold. Tossing his knife in the air, he watched the man opposite, who removed his own mask to reveal unruly black hair jutting in every direction, sharp as blades.
“You’ve done better than I expected, making it this far,” the blond said.
“Praise from Caesar. An honor,” the black-haired young man replied coolly.

“But this is as far as you go.” The instant he spoke, Caesar shot forward like an arrow. An invisible pressure seemed to rush toward Lu Mingfei with him, making his heart tremble and his breathing stop. Caesar blurred with unbelievable speed, an eagle diving from the heights. His knife and the arm holding it vanished into an even greater speed, rendering the blade nearly invisible!
This was a stroke meant to kill. Hard, ruthless, bearing an emperor’s imposing majesty. Even a block of iron before it would have split.

But Chu Zihang wasn’t iron. The iron was in his hand. He stood still, sweeping his long sword slowly through an arc and holding it in midair. Caesar’s almost certain killing stroke approached. Instantly, Chu’s blade vanished, too. A flick of the wrist sent it flashing against Caesar’s knife tip with modest force. This was skill beyond strength and speed. A blade was a lever; force at its tip transmitted maximum strain to the wielder’s wrist. Chu struck the instant before Caesar exerted his full power—his weakest moment. He intercepted the attack!

Lu Mingfei couldn’t follow the details. He saw Caesar reach Chu, who held his stance and shifted only his upper body. Caesar seemed to hit a wall. He stumbled slightly, leaned backward, then retreated several quick steps.
Chu had blocked that imperial pressure. Suddenly, Lu Mingfei could breathe again.

Metal hummed. Chu’s long blade vibrated violently. Though it had touched the knife only for an instant, the tremendous impact set its tamahagane steel quivering like a plucked brass reed. Caesar’s power was so great that the sword was dissipating it through vibration.
Chu backed away and examined his blade. “Murasame still falls short of Dictator.”
A moment’s stillness. Then they lunged again.

Dictator was fierce and unyielding in Caesar’s hand. Chu’s Murasame melted into the air like a phantom, suddenly flashing out in lethal slashes. Whenever Dictator intercepted it, it withdrew instantly and dissolved into a nearly invisible streak. Their desperate duel was graceful as a dance, too swift for Lu Mingfei to follow. A blurred black figure, a blurred dark-red one, Dictator’s shadow, Murasame’s dazzling reflected sunlight—all mingled beyond separation.
The sword’s humming grew fiercer, mingling with Caesar’s roars. Murderous intent thickened the air.
“Dictator? Murasame? What is this?” Lu Mingfei muttered.

Dictator meant the ancient Roman office of dictator. Murasame was a sword that shouldn’t exist outside Japanese games. Supposedly, after killing a thousand people, the famed Muramasa blade transformed into the demonic Murasame, which shed rain to wash off the blood after killing. But Lu Mingfei had looked it up. An Edo-period writer, Kyokutei Bakin, had invented the sword in Nansō Satomi Hakkenden. And here someone had actually drawn it.
Could this get any more absurd? Caesar, my man, can you pull Frostmourne out from behind your back next? he thought as he lay there.
Faint footsteps came from behind him in the passage. He paused, ears pricking slightly.

They approached slowly. He suddenly realized the person might have a gun. Before he could leap up, raise both hands, and say, I surrender! Innocent passerby! a foot landed on his back. Its owner sprang lightly over him and out of the passage. The foot had hit over his lungs, forcing out a breath and an involuntary “Ow!” Startled, the person drew a Colt from her waist, spun into a crouch, then dropped cross-legged to aim behind her.
Their eyes met. He blinked. Those lovely, spirited eyes were startlingly familiar. So were the dark-red ponytail and swaying four-leaf-clover earrings.
“Come on, little bunny. Have a hug!” A voice sounded in his head. These were the eyes that had watched him then, so beautiful they frightened him.
“Nono, it’s me!” He brightened. Apart from the two lunatics still fighting with blades, the last living person here was Nono.

She wore dark-red combat gear. He paused, realizing she was part of this battle: Red’s last girl besides Caesar. Caesar’s challenge had concealed an ambush. The last fighter would infiltrate Black’s headquarters. Nono was his hidden arrow. Lu Mingfei realized he scarcely knew her. They had spent only a few hours together. Yet all the way across the ocean, it was this almost-stranger who had given him peace of mind.
Why trust her? Perhaps because there was no one else to trust.
And now she was pointing a gun at him.
He cautiously raised his hands. “Don’t shoot… I surrender… I’m… just passing through.”
Her gun stayed level. Not even an eyebrow moved.
“Senior… I, I…” he said.
A faint smile appeared at her lips. Suddenly she shouted, “Down!”
Without a moment’s hesitation, she pulled the trigger.
The bullet screamed over his head, missing it by a hair. At her shout, he had clutched his head and dropped flat.
That damned, inexplicable trust. She was pointing a gun at him, and still he obeyed without thinking.

Blood spread across her chest, turning the dark-red uniform black. A large-caliber sniper round had struck her squarely. Its force nearly toppled her backward, but with her last strength she held herself upright.
She looked down at the wound and nodded to him, her voice hoarse. “Obedient enough. Still too slow…”

He turned. A girl in black lay flat on the ground with a sniper rifle, smoke curling from its dark muzzle. He recognized an American Barrett M82A1, the “King of Snipers,” in .50 caliber. At this range, anyone hit was beyond saving. The bullet would turn their organs to bloody pulp.

She was Black’s last fighter, the star sniper. She had jumped from a side window into the passage. Nono could have shot her, but Lu Mingfei blocked her line of fire. They had faced off like cowboys, and Nono had fired a fraction of a second too late. Lu Mingfei… had been too slow.
He couldn’t believe his eyes, but the blood pouring down her chest said it was real. Her gaze unfocused. Signs of death appeared.

He seized his head. Pain tore through it as though something deep inside were drilling its way out. Darkness swallowed his vision. Brilliant golden eyes opened against it, and a bell-like voice asked, “Will you trade?”
Trade? Trade what?
A dim impulse urged him to agree. Somehow, agreeing would make things different. The instant he accepted, something would change.

The sniper sprang up, abandoned her rifle, and drew a combat knife from her lower back. Before Lu Mingfei could react, she stepped on his back and landed lightly beside Nono. Grabbing her hair, she drove the knife into her throat. Thick, reeking blood splashed over Nono’s face. A few drops struck his.
“We won! Caesar! You lost!” The girl raised her bloody blade.

They had indeed won. Neither Caesar nor Chu could break free of their duel. She could stroll into Red’s headquarters humming a tune and win this murderous game. If it were a game of Go, they had reached the endgame. The outcome could no longer change.
But a red stone appeared at the point of their ko fight.

A deafening gunshot drowned out her cry. A bullet from behind drove her forward with tremendous momentum. Disbelieving, she struggled to turn. Lu Mingfei was silently rising, holding Toyama’s abandoned PPK, the pistol modified into an aircraft cannon.
That red stone caught fire.

Caesar and Chu broke apart together and looked toward the smoke-filled passage. An unsteady figure emerged, carrying the heavy King of Snipers. The rifle was nearly a meter and a half long and looked absurdly awkward in his hand. He wasn’t carrying it like anyone with training.
Caesar frowned. “Who are you? Nonparticipants, out!”
